q: In evaluating a decision tree, the correct procedure is to:

options.A: Work backwards from the terminal nodes, taking expected values at chance nodes and the best alternative at decision nodes
options.B: Work forwards from the first decision, taking the highest outcome at every node
options.C: Ignore the probabilities and add all the outcomes
options.D: Select the branch with the highest single outcome

q: The simulation (Monte Carlo) technique of project risk analysis consists of:

options.A: Varying one project variable at a time while holding the others constant
options.B: Preparing the best, worst and most likely estimates of the net present value
options.C: Interviewing experts to estimate the probabilities of outcomes
options.D: Repeatedly drawing values of the key variables from their probability distributions to build up a probability distribution of the project's net present value

q: Where capital rationing extends over several periods, with the funds available in one period depending on the projects accepted in earlier periods, simple ranking of projects by profitability index becomes unreliable and the selection is best made by:

options.A: The payback period method
options.B: Mathematical programming techniques
options.C: The average rate of return method
options.D: Accepting the largest projects first

q: Head-office administrative costs, apportioned to a proposed project on a notional basis, will remain unchanged whether or not the project is accepted. In the project's appraisal, these costs should be:

options.A: Excluded, as they are not incremental to the project
options.B: Included in full, as every project must bear overheads
options.C: Included at one-half of the apportioned amount
options.D: Treated as the project's sunk cost

q: In the economic (social cost-benefit) appraisal of a public project, the social discount rate is used because it represents:

options.A: The rate of interest charged by banks on project loans
options.B: The market rate of return on government securities
options.C: The rate of inflation expected over the project life
options.D: The rate at which society values future benefits and costs in terms of present benefits and costs

q: A project has a profitability index of 1.25 and a net present value of (+) Rs 2,00,000. Its initial outlay is:
The net credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 24,00,000 and its average collection period is 2 months. Its average trade debtors are:
The current liabilities of an enterprise are Rs 4,00,000. Its current ratio is 2.5 : 1 and its quick ratio is 1.5 : 1. There are no prepaid expenses. The value of its stock is:

The debt-equity ratio (long-term debt to shareholders' funds) of an enterprise is 3 : 2 and its capital employed, comprising long-term debt and shareholders' funds, is Rs 20,00,000. Its long-term debt is:
The average inventory of an enterprise is held for 73 days of the year (365 days). Its inventory turnover ratio is:

options.A: 7.3 times
options.B: 4.93 times
options.C: 5 times
options.D: 6 times

q: A railway's return on its capital-at-charge is 6% and the capital-at-charge is Rs 1,20,000 crore. Its net earnings are:

options.A: Rs 20,000 crore
options.B: Rs 7,200 crore
options.C: Rs 6,000 crore
options.D: Rs 72,000 crore

q: A company's share is quoted at Rs 420 and its price-earnings ratio is 14. Its earnings per share are:

options.A: Rs 30
options.B: Rs 14
options.D: Rs 15

q: A company has earnings per share of Rs 18 and its share is quoted in the market at Rs 225. Its earnings yield is:
An enterprise has a return on equity of 16% and a dividend payout ratio of 25%. Its sustainable growth rate, computed as return on equity multiplied by the retention ratio, is:

The defensive (liquid) assets of an enterprise amount to Rs 4,50,000 and its operating expenses for the year are Rs 36,50,000. Its defensive interval (defensive assets divided by average daily operating expenses, on a 365-day year) is:

options.A: 30 days
options.B: 60 days
options.C: 45 days
options.D: 15 days

q: The net worth of an enterprise, which has equity share capital of Rs 10,00,000 and reserves and surplus of Rs 6,50,000, and carries preliminary expenses of Rs 50,000 as a fictitious asset, is:
The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 8,00,000, its total assets are Rs 52,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 12,00,000. Its return on capital employed is:
A company has 2,00,000 equity shares quoted at Rs 240 per share and annual sales of Rs 12,00,00,000. Its price-to-sales ratio (market capitalisation divided by annual sales) is:
An enterprise purchases stock for cash. The immediate effect of this transaction is that:

options.A: Both the current ratio and the quick ratio fall
options.B: The current ratio rises and the quick ratio is unchanged
options.C: The current ratio is unchanged and the quick ratio falls
options.D: Both the ratios remain unchanged

q: An enterprise has current assets of Rs 3,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs 3,75,000 (current ratio 0.8 : 1). It pays Rs 75,000 in cash to its trade creditors. Its current ratio will:

options.A: Fall to 0.75 : 1
options.B: Rise to 0.85 : 1
options.C: Remain unchanged at 0.8 : 1
options.D: Rise to 1 : 1

q: Over a year, the current ratio of an enterprise has improved but its quick ratio has deteriorated. The most likely explanation is:

options.A: A large collection of dues from trade debtors
options.B: A fall in the level of stock held
options.C: A repayment of long-term loans
options.D: A build-up of stock, possibly including slow-moving items

q: The sales of an enterprise have risen substantially during the year, but its gross profit ratio has declined while its inventory turnover ratio has improved. The most likely explanation is:

options.A: An increase in the selling prices of its products
options.B: A reduction in selling prices to expand the volume of sales
options.C: Overvaluation of the closing stock
options.D: A fall in the volume of sales

q: The fixed assets ratio (net fixed assets divided by long-term funds) of an enterprise is 0.8. This indicates that:

options.A: Long-term funds finance the whole of the fixed assets and a part of the working capital as well
options.B: A part of the fixed assets has been financed out of current liabilities
options.C: The enterprise has no working capital
options.D: The fixed assets are over-valued

q: The market price to book value ratio of a company's share is 1.5. This indicates that:

options.A: The share is quoted at a discount to its book value
options.B: The book value per share is higher than the market price
options.C: The market values the company's equity above the book value of its net assets
options.D: The company is over-capitalised

q: Over three years, an enterprise's average collection period has lengthened, its inventory turnover has fallen and the period it takes to pay its creditors has stretched well beyond the agreed terms. Taken together, these trends most clearly indicate:

options.A: A steady improvement in profitability
options.B: Growing strain on working capital and liquidity
options.C: A deliberate policy of reducing stock levels
options.D: An improvement in the quality of its debtors

q: A company declares a dividend which remains unpaid at the balance sheet date. The immediate effect of the declaration on its current ratio is that the ratio:

options.A: Rises, because reserves have been converted into share capital
options.B: Is unchanged, because no cash has moved
options.C: Rises, because current liabilities fall
options.D: Falls, because the dividend payable increases current liabilities while current assets are unchanged

q: A company issues bonus shares by capitalising a part of its general reserve. The effect of the issue is that:

options.A: Total proprietors' funds remain unchanged, while book value per share and earnings per share fall as the number of shares increases
options.B: Total proprietors' funds increase by the value of the bonus shares
options.C: Working capital increases by the value of the bonus shares
options.D: Earnings per share rise because reserves have fallen

q: The proprietary ratio of an enterprise is 0.55. Its debt ratio, computed as total debt (total outside liabilities) divided by total assets, is:
The total return earned by a shareholder on a share over a period consists of:

options.A: The dividend yield only
options.B: The capital appreciation in the share price only
options.C: The earnings yield of the share
options.D: The dividend yield together with the capital appreciation yield

q: An enterprise revalues its fixed assets upwards by Rs 5,00,000, creating a revaluation reserve of the same amount, its proprietors' funds being Rs 15,00,000 and total assets Rs 25,00,000 before the revaluation. The effect on its proprietary ratio is that the ratio:

options.A: Falls, because total assets have increased
options.B: Remains unchanged at 0.60
options.C: Falls to 0.50
options.D: Rises, from 0.60 to about 0.67, as proprietors' funds and total assets increase by the same amount

q: The plant utilisation budget of a manufacturing enterprise primarily shows:

options.A: The expenditure to be incurred on repairs and maintenance of plant during the budget period
options.B: The budgeted hours for which the available plant capacity is planned to be utilised during the period, providing the basis for the production programme and the production overhead budget
options.C: The new plant and machinery proposed to be purchased during the budget period
options.D: The depreciation to be charged on the plant during the budget period

q: A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 12,000, estimated receipts of Rs 1,85,000 and estimated payments of Rs 2,30,000. The enterprise must maintain a minimum cash balance of Rs 15,000, and any borrowing can be made only in multiples of Rs 5,000. The amount it will need to borrow during the month is:

Budgeted production is 19,000 units and each unit requires 2.5 hours of productive labour time. Normal idle time is expected to be 5% of the gross (paid) labour hours. The direct labour budget should provide for gross labour hours of:

options.A: 47,500 hours
options.B: 49,875 hours
options.C: 45,125 hours
options.D: 50,000 hours

q: In preparing the sales budget, the budgeted sales value is arrived at after deducting:

options.A: Trade discount allowed to buyers, because it reduces the invoice price itself; cash discount is not deducted from sales, being treated separately as a financial item
options.B: Cash discount expected to be allowed to prompt-paying customers only
options.C: Both trade discount and cash discount, in every case
options.D: Neither trade discount nor any other allowance of any kind

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 1,20,000 and variable costs of Rs 10 per unit. In addition, supervision cost of Rs 12,000 is incurred for every 6,000 units of output or part thereof. The total flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 24,000 units is:
In budgetary control, the production volume ratio, also called the activity ratio, is equal to:

options.A: The capacity ratio multiplied by the calendar ratio
options.B: The efficiency ratio divided by the capacity ratio
options.C: The efficiency ratio multiplied by the capacity ratio
options.D: The calendar ratio plus the efficiency ratio

q: The correct distinction between a budget centre and a cost centre is that:

options.A: The two terms mean exactly the same thing and are interchangeable
options.B: A budget centre can never contain more than one cost centre
options.C: A cost centre is defined for budgetary control, while a budget centre is defined only for collecting costs
options.D: A budget centre is a section of the organisation defined for the purpose of budgetary control under a responsible manager and may cover revenue and capital expenditure as well as costs, often comprising several cost centres, whereas a cost centre is a location, function or item of equipment to which costs are charged for cost ascertainment and control

q: Towards the close of the financial year, a departmental manager hurriedly spends the unspent balance of his budget on items of low priority, mainly because he fears that his budget for the next year will be cut if the amount remains unspent this year. This behaviour is best described as:

options.A: A dysfunctional effect of budgetary control, in which the budget comes to be treated as an entitlement to spend, arising when future allocations are linked to past spending and unspent balances lapse
options.B: Budgetary slack, deliberately built into the budget at the time of its preparation
options.C: The normal working of a rolling budget
options.D: Zero-based ranking of decision packages

q: The correct relationship between the materials usage budget and the materials purchase budget is that:

options.A: The purchase budget is prepared first and the usage budget is derived from it
options.B: The two budgets state the same quantity in every case
options.C: The materials usage budget, derived from the production budget and the standard consumption per unit, states the quantity to be consumed, while the purchase budget adjusts this quantity for the opening and closing stocks of material to state the quantity to be bought
options.D: The usage budget is prepared by the purchase department and the purchase budget by the production department

q: Machinery was purchased in the previous year on deferred payment terms, and the final instalment for it is paid during the current year. The correct treatment of this instalment is that it:

options.A: Appears both as a payment in the current year's cash budget and as an expense in the current year's budgeted profit and loss account
options.B: Appears as a payment in the current year's cash budget, but is not charged as an expense in the current year's budgeted profit and loss account, only the depreciation on the machinery being so charged
options.C: Appears in neither the cash budget nor the budgeted profit and loss account of the current year
options.D: Appears only as an expense in the current year's budgeted profit and loss account

q: A supplementary budget, in budgetary control, is a budget which is:

options.A: Another name for the master budget of the enterprise
options.B: Prepared only for the cash transactions of the enterprise
options.C: Prepared by government departments alone, for obtaining additional grants from the legislature
options.D: Prepared during the budget period when a material change in the conditions or in the principal budget factor makes the original budget unrealistic for the remaining part of the period, so that the working plan for that part has to be supplemented and recast

q: Which of the following correctly states a limitation of budgetary control?

options.A: Budgetary control by itself does not prevent inefficiency or waste; it only provides targets, measures performance against them and reveals deviations promptly, and the actual improvement depends on the corrective action taken by management
options.B: Budgetary control automatically eliminates all waste in an enterprise
options.C: Budgetary control is a substitute for management itself
options.D: Budgetary control guarantees that the budgeted profit will necessarily be earned

q: A short-term budget (current budget) is best described as:

options.A: A budget prepared at very short notice in an emergency
options.B: A budget which covers only the cash receipts and payments of an enterprise
options.C: A budget covering a short period, usually not exceeding one year, subdivided into monthly or weekly sections and subject to frequent revision, as distinct from long-term budgets which may cover several years
options.D: A zero-based budget prepared for a single department

q: For budgetary control to motivate managers instead of discouraging them, the budget targets should be set at a level which is:

options.A: Impossible to achieve, so that managers are kept under maximum pressure at all times
options.B: Challenging but attainable under efficient working, because targets that cannot possibly be reached demotivate managers, while targets set too low encourage slack and poor performance
options.C: So low that every manager can achieve them without any effort
options.D: Fixed without any regard to what is attainable in practice

q: From the standpoint of the short-term creditors of an enterprise, a positive net working capital is significant mainly because it represents:

options.A: The profit earned by the enterprise during the year
options.B: The cash balance held by the enterprise on the balance sheet date
options.C: Proof that the enterprise has used no short-term funds at all
options.D: The cushion or margin of safety available to them, being the extent by which current assets exceed current liabilities, indicating that current claims can be met even if some current assets realise less than their book value

q: Under the turnover method recommended by the Nayak Committee for assessing the working capital of small borrowers, the total working capital requirement is assessed at:

options.A: 25% of the projected annual turnover, of which the bank finances 20% of the turnover and the borrower brings in 5% of the turnover as his own margin
options.B: 20% of the projected annual turnover, the whole of it being financed by the bank
options.C: 25% of the fixed assets of the borrower
options.D: The amount worked out from the length of the operating cycle alone, turnover being irrelevant

q: The projected annual turnover of a small enterprise is Rs 60,00,000. On the Nayak Committee turnover method, the borrower's own contribution (margin) towards its working capital requirement is:
For estimating the working capital requirement of an enterprise, the amount to be shown against debtors is generally taken at:

options.A: The selling price of the goods sold on credit, because the profit element must also be financed in full
options.B: The market price of the goods on the date of estimation
options.C: Cost, that is, the cost of the goods sold on credit, because the profit element included in the selling price does not have to be financed by the enterprise
options.D: Nil, because debtors are not considered in estimating working capital

q: An enterprise has 10,000 units in work-in-progress. The material cost is Rs 20 per unit and the material is fully introduced at the start of the process. The labour cost is Rs 10 per unit and the overheads are Rs 10 per unit, and the units in process are on an average 50% complete as regards labour and overheads. The funds blocked in work-in-progress are:

The total annual cost of an enterprise is Rs 26,00,000, which includes depreciation of Rs 2,60,000. Its operating cycle is 54 days, reckoning a year of 360 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
Advances received from customers, as commonly happens where goods are made to order or have long delivery periods, affect the working capital of an enterprise in that they:

options.A: Increase the working capital to be provided by the enterprise itself
options.B: Are a source of working capital finance which reduces the funds the enterprise itself must provide for carrying on its operations
options.C: Are a form of long-term share capital of the enterprise
options.D: Are shown among the current assets of the enterprise

q:
Consider the following statements about inter-corporate deposits and public deposits as sources of finance:
1. Inter-corporate deposits are unsecured short-term deposits placed by one company with another company.
2. Public deposits are amounts raised directly from the public for fixed periods, without the security of any assets.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: The correct distinction between commercial paper and a certificate of deposit is that:

options.A: Commercial paper is an unsecured promissory note issued by a company to raise short-term funds, whereas a certificate of deposit is issued by a bank or a financial institution acknowledging a deposit of money with it for a specified period
options.B: Commercial paper is issued by banks, whereas a certificate of deposit is issued by manufacturing companies
options.C: Both are issued only by the Reserve Bank of India
options.D: A certificate of deposit is a long-term security, whereas commercial paper is a share

q: An enterprise whose sales are steadily contracting from year to year will, other things being equal, experience that:

options.A: Its working capital requirement rises continuously because of the falling sales
options.B: There is no change at all in its working capital requirement
options.C: It must borrow more and more to finance its working capital
options.D: Funds previously locked up in stocks and debtors are progressively released as the scale of operations shrinks, so that its working capital requirement falls

q: Which of the following is NOT a carrying (holding) cost of inventory held as a part of working capital?

options.A: Interest on the funds locked up in the inventory
options.B: The cost of placing purchase orders and expediting deliveries from suppliers
options.C: Storage, warehousing and insurance charges for the stock held
options.D: Losses from obsolescence and deterioration of the stock held

q: The operating cycle of a purely service enterprise, such as a consultancy or a transport undertaking rendering services, differs from that of a manufacturing enterprise mainly in that:

options.A: It is always longer than the operating cycle of every manufacturing enterprise
options.B: The enterprise requires no working capital at all
options.C: It has no raw material and finished goods stock stages, so that the funds of the enterprise remain locked up mainly in the cost of services rendered but not yet billed or collected, that is, in debtors
options.D: It consists only of the period of credit allowed by its suppliers

q: An enterprise shows a very high working capital turnover ratio (annual sales divided by net working capital). The sound interpretation of this position is that:

options.A: It may indicate overtrading on an inadequate working capital base, with attendant liquidity strain, and not necessarily superior efficiency
options.B: It always proves that the working capital management of the enterprise is ideal
options.C: It indicates that the enterprise carries excessive working capital
options.D: It indicates that the enterprise has necessarily made losses during the year

q: In estimating working capital by the components method, a margin for contingencies is added to the estimated net working capital in order to:

options.A: Increase the profit of the enterprise by the amount of the margin
options.B: Satisfy a percentage prescribed in the Companies Act for this purpose
options.C: Reduce the working capital to be arranged from the bank
options.D: Provide for unforeseen increases, such as a rise in the prices of materials, delays in collecting from debtors and other emergencies, over and above the requirement worked out on the expected figures

q: As compared to a mass-production enterprise with a continuous and steady cycle of operations, an enterprise producing goods only against the individual orders of customers will generally require working capital which is:

options.A: Nil, because it holds no work-in-progress at any time
options.B: Comparatively higher in relation to its scale of operations and harder to estimate, because funds remain locked up in varied work-in-progress for longer and less predictable periods
options.C: Always exactly equal to that of a mass-production enterprise of the same size
options.D: Required only for holding finished goods, and for no other purpose

q: The credit sales of an enterprise during a year are Rs 9,60,000. Its trade debtors were Rs 1,20,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 1,50,000 at the end of the year. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash received from customers during the year is:

The credit purchases of an enterprise during a year are Rs 7,20,000. Its trade creditors were Rs 90,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 1,10,000 at the end of the year. The cash paid to suppliers during the year is:
In a cash flow statement, the net increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents during a period is equal to:

options.A: The funds from operations of the enterprise for the period
options.B: The algebraic sum of the net cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities, so that the statement reconciles the opening balance of cash and cash equivalents with the closing balance
options.C: The net profit earned by the enterprise during the period
options.D: The net change in the working capital of the enterprise during the period

q: Where the provision for taxation is treated as a current liability in preparing a fund flow statement, the correct treatment is that:

options.A: The income-tax paid during the year is shown separately as an application of funds
options.B: The provision made during the year is added back to the net profit in computing the funds from operations
options.C: The provision for taxation is excluded altogether from the schedule of changes in working capital
options.D: The provision is taken in the schedule of changes in working capital as a current liability, and the income-tax paid during the year is not shown separately as an application of funds, its effect being captured through the movement in that current liability

q: The discount on the issue of debentures, to the extent written off in the profit and loss account during a year, is dealt with in computing the funds from operations by:

options.A: Deducting it from the net profit of the year
options.B: Showing it as an application of funds in the fund flow statement
options.C: Adding it back to the net profit, like other non-cash and fictitious write-offs, because the write-off involves no outflow of funds during the year
options.D: Ignoring it in the cash flow statement but treating it as a source of funds

q: An enterprise has made a net loss of Rs 40,000 during a year, after charging depreciation of Rs 90,000 and goodwill written off of Rs 10,000, and after crediting a profit of Rs 25,000 on the sale of its investments. Its funds from operations are:

Bad debts of earlier years, which had been written off, are recovered in cash during the current year by a non-financial enterprise. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, the amount recovered is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities, being a receipt arising in the course of its trading operations and credited as income
options.B: Investing activities
options.C: Financing activities
options.D: No activity, because a recovery is never a cash flow

q: Compensation is received from the insurers for finished goods destroyed by fire. For the purposes of the cash flow statement under AS-3, this receipt is reported as a cash flow from:

options.A: Investing activities, as is every receipt under an insurance claim
options.B: Financing activities
options.C: No activity at all, because the receipt arises out of a loss
options.D: Operating activities, because it compensates for stock, an operating item, unlike compensation for a fixed asset destroyed, which is reported under investing activities

q: Under AS-3, where an item of income-tax is specifically identifiable with an investing or a financing transaction, for example the tax attributable to the gain on the sale of plant, that tax is classified in the cash flow statement:

options.A: Under operating activities in every case, without exception
options.B: Under financing activities in every case
options.C: Under the same activity as the transaction to which it relates, and not under operating activities, taxes not so identifiable being classified under operating activities
options.D: It is excluded from the cash flow statement altogether

q: In a cash flow statement under AS-3, the effect of changes in exchange rates on cash and cash equivalents held in a foreign currency is presented:

options.A: As a part of the cash flows from operating activities
options.B: Separately, as a reconciling item between the opening and the closing balances of cash and cash equivalents, and not as a part of the operating, investing or financing cash flows
options.C: It is ignored altogether in the statement
options.D: As a part of the cash flows from investing activities

q: Under AS-3, certain cash flows may be reported on a net basis instead of on a gross basis. This net reporting is permitted for:

options.A: Items characterised by quick turnover, large amounts and short maturities, and for cash receipts and payments made on behalf of customers where the flows reflect the customer's activity rather than the enterprise's own
options.B: All cash flows of every enterprise, without any condition
options.C: Only the income-tax paid by the enterprise
options.D: No cash flow at all, netting being prohibited in every case

q: An enterprise buys back its own equity shares from the market and pays cash to the shareholders for them. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, this payment is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities
options.B: Investing activities
options.C: No activity, because the transaction concerns its own shares
options.D: Financing activities, being a return of capital to the owners of the enterprise

q: In a fund flow statement, an increase in the bank overdraft of an enterprise during a year is dealt with by:

options.A: Showing the increase as a source of funds in the fund flow statement
options.B: Showing the increase as an application of funds in the fund flow statement
options.C: Taking the overdraft as a current liability in the schedule of changes in working capital, where its increase decreases the working capital, and not showing it as a source of funds, sources being confined to non-current transactions
options.D: Ignoring the overdraft completely, both in the statement and in the schedule

q: Where debentures are issued for cash at a discount, the amount shown as a source of funds in the fund flow statement is:

options.A: The face value of the debentures issued
options.B: The net amount actually received, that is, the face value less the discount on the issue
options.C: The face value plus the discount on the issue
options.D: Only the amount of the discount on the issue

q: Under AS-3, investments in equity shares are normally excluded from 'cash equivalents' in a cash flow statement mainly because:

options.A: They are subject to a significant risk of change in value, whereas a cash equivalent must be subject to only an insignificant risk of such change, an equity investment qualifying only in exceptional cases, as where it is acquired shortly before its redemption
options.B: Equity shares are always long-term investments of the enterprise
options.C: Equity shares can never be sold in the market at short notice
options.D: The Companies Act prohibits their being treated as investments

q: An important limitation of the cash flow statement, which makes the fund flow statement a useful supplement to it, is that the cash flow statement:

options.A: Is prohibited by law for companies
options.B: Shows the working capital position better than the fund flow statement
options.C: Treats depreciation as an actual outflow of cash
options.D: Is confined to the movement of cash alone and ignores significant non-cash transactions and the changes in the other components of working capital, so that by itself it does not show how the long-term activities of the enterprise have been financed

q: An imputed (notional) cost in cost accounting is a cost which:

options.A: Has actually been paid in cash during the current period
options.B: Does not involve any actual cash outlay, but is taken into account as a hypothetical charge — such as interest on the firm's own capital or rent of premises owned by the firm — so that costs and decisions are not distorted
options.C: Is estimated by the works manager without reference to any records
options.D: Is charged only in the financial accounts and never in the cost accounts

q: The profit as per cost accounts is Rs 2,50,000. In reconciling it with the financial accounts, the following are found: factory overheads were over-absorbed in the cost accounts by Rs 18,000; notional rent of own premises was charged in the cost accounts only, Rs 15,000; dividend received, appearing only in the financial books, is Rs 22,000; and income tax provided in the financial books is Rs 40,000. The profit as per the financial accounts is:

In a reconciliation of cost and financial accounts starting from the profit as per cost accounts, the fact that the closing stock has been valued Rs 12,000 higher in the cost accounts than in the financial accounts requires that the amount be:

options.A: Deducted, because the higher stock valuation in the cost accounts has reduced the cost of goods sold there and so inflated the cost profit
options.B: Added, because a higher stock value always increases the financial profit
options.C: Ignored, because stock valuation never affects the profit of either set of books
options.D: Added to the opening stock of the next period in the financial books only

q: A cost manual of a factory is a document which:

options.A: Records the actual cost incurred on each job during the year
options.B: Contains the price list at which the products of the factory are sold
options.C: Is the statutory audit report on the cost accounts of the factory
options.D: Sets out the costing system of the organisation — the procedures, forms, methods of collecting and classifying costs and the duties of the staff concerned — so that cost work is done uniformly

q: A materials abstract (analysis sheet of material issues) prepared periodically in the cost office serves mainly to:

options.A: Summarise and analyse all material requisitions of the period job-wise and department-wise, so that the total issues can be posted to the cost ledger and charged to the jobs and overhead accounts concerned
options.B: Record the physical balance of each item of material lying in the stores
options.C: Fix the price at which materials are to be purchased from suppliers
options.D: Replace the stores ledger maintained in the cost office

q: A supplementary overhead rate is used to dispose of under-absorbed or over-absorbed overheads when:

options.A: The amount involved is very small and arises from ordinary estimation differences
options.B: The amount involved is material and has arisen from abnormal circumstances or an error in fixing the absorption rate, so that it is spread over the work-in-progress, finished stock and cost of sales instead of being written off wholly to profit
options.C: The factory has worked at exactly its budgeted capacity throughout the year
options.D: The overheads of the year have been absorbed in full with no balance remaining

q: Factory overheads of a period are under-absorbed by Rs 72,000 and the difference is disposed of by a supplementary rate.
